# Job Shop Quote: full text

Job Shop Quote is a hosted web app for CNC machine shops and metal fabrication job shops, open for sign-up at https://jobshop-quote.marisstella.app/sign-up. A shop sets up its rate card (machine and setup rates, material priced by weight, piece or length, outside processing, markups, minimums and quantity breaks), adds an RFQ's parts and files, and gets each line priced only from those rates, with setup and cycle times from its routings and from STEP and DXF measurements that the estimator can correct. It builds the quote PDF, emails it when the estimator sends it, gives the customer a link to accept or decline, reminds about follow-ups and expiring quotes, prints job travelers and keeps a won/lost log. An estimator at the shop reviews and sends every quote; the product never sends quotes itself. The Early access plan is free (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Built but not switched on in the hosted app yet: reading RFQ emails and PDF drawings with AI, RFQs forwarded by email, paid plans, the QuickBooks Online connection. It has no customers yet. It is not set up for CUI or export-controlled (ITAR/EAR) drawings.

## Work through the RFQ backlog without hiring another estimator.

Set your machine rates, setup charges, material prices and markups once. Add an RFQ's parts,
attach its STEP or DXF files, and Job Shop Quote prices every line from your rates, measures what the
CAD files can tell it, and builds the quote PDF for your estimator to check and send. Nothing goes
to a customer until you send it.

- Prices come from your rate table, never from a guess
- Every line shows which of your rates it used
- Quantity breaks, minimums and markups applied the same way every time

See how it works

How the price is built, step by step →

### The quoting pile is the bottleneck nobody hired for

In a job shop, quoting usually lands on the owner or one estimator. Every RFQ means opening the
email, reading each drawing, working out stock, setups and cycle times, looking up material and outside
processing, and applying your rates. That work happens between running the floor and answering the
phone, and while RFQs wait, the customers who sent them wait too.

Job Shop Quote does the arithmetic and the paperwork, so your estimator's time goes on the judgment calls: the tricky features, the quantity breaks, and whether you want the job.

### What it does, and what stays yours

#### Job Shop Quote does the legwork

- Reads RFQ emails and PDF drawings: parts, quantities, material, finish, tolerances and notes (AI reading: not switched on yet)

- Checks what it read a second time against the drawing and flags anything it can't confirm (AI reading: not switched on yet)

- Measures STEP, IGES, STL and DXF files: blank size, holes, cut length, pierces and bends, for roughing, drilling, cutting and bending times you can correct

- Applies your rates, minimums and markups with plain arithmetic: same inputs, same price

- Lists the sent quotes due for a follow-up each morning and keeps a log of every call, so no quote goes quiet

- Dates every material price, warns when one is past your limit, and lists the open quotes priced before your supplier's price moved

- Puts your won jobs on your machines by due date, shows which ones run past their date, and gives each new quote a lead time from your real backlog

- Imports your supplier's price sheet showing each price change and the open quotes it touches before you save, and keeps the supplier and date in each price's history

#### Your shop keeps control

- Your rate table sets every price; corrections your estimator makes become shop rules

- Your estimator reviews every line and decides what gets quoted

- Quotes are never sent automatically

- Your drawings and rates are never used to train AI models

## How it works

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/how-it-works

How it works

## From an RFQ in your inbox to a quote your estimator trusts

This is how Job Shop Quote works. It is new, and the first shops on it shape what it does next, so details may change; this page will change with them. Steps marked as not switched on yet are built but off in the hosted app.

-

### 1Set up your rates once

You enter how your shop prices work: each machine or work center and its hourly rate,
setup charges, material costs or markups, outside processes such as anodizing, plating or heat treat
with what your vendors charge, minimum order values, quantity breaks and how you round. This rate
table is the only place prices come from. Not sure what an hour on a machine costs you?
Work out a machine's hourly rate.

-

### 2Send in the RFQ

Forward the customer's email to your shop's intake address, or upload the PDF drawings
directly. It reads email text and PDF drawings, including scans, and CAD files: a STEP solid's size,
volume and holes, an IGES solid's size and holes, an STL mesh's size and volume, and a DXF flat pattern's cut length, pierces and bend lines. From those it suggests
the blank, the parts per sheet and, where you have entered the rate, a roughing, drilling, tapping, cutting or bending time, each labelled with
how it was worked out. Native SolidWorks files are stored but not measured yet.

RFQs by email to a shop address are not switched on in the hosted app yet: upload the files instead.

Reading RFQ emails and PDF drawings with AI is built but not switched on in the hosted app yet. Until it is, the app reads them by fixed rules: labelled lines (Part number, Qty, Material, Finish, Due) and parts tables with a header row, each value shown with the line it came from. You check those and enter the rest yourself.

-

### 3It reads the drawing, then checks itself

For each part it pulls out material, stock size, features, tolerances, finish, quantity
and due date. A second, separate pass checks every extracted value against the drawing. A value it
can't confirm, like a smudged tolerance or a missing material callout, is flagged for your estimator
with the page it came from. It is never filled in with a guess.

Reading RFQ emails and PDF drawings with AI is built but not switched on in the hosted app yet. Until it is, the app reads them by fixed rules: labelled lines (Part number, Qty, Material, Finish, Due) and parts tables with a header row, each value shown with the line it came from. You check those and enter the rest yourself.

-

### 4Priced by your rules

Setup and cycle-time estimates are the hard part of quoting, so Job Shop Quote proposes them
with its reasoning written out (operations, tools, approximate times) for your estimator to accept
or correct. The dollar figures are then plain arithmetic on your rate table: the same inputs always
give the same price, and every line shows which rate it used. Corrections your estimator makes are
saved as rules for your shop, so the next similar part starts closer.

-

### 5Your estimator reviews and sends

The draft quote lists every part, its price build-up and anything flagged. Your
estimator edits what needs editing and approves it. You then download it as a PDF on your letterhead
or have Job Shop Quote email it from your estimator's send button. It never sends a quote on its own.
With it can go a link where the customer picks a quantity and accepts, with a PO number, or
declines; the answer shows on the quote, which is marked won or lost.

### Each part of the app

- CNC quoting software: Price machined parts from your own rate card: setup and cycle per operation, material, outside processing, minimums and quantity breaks, as a quote PDF.
- Sheet metal quoting software: Quote laser, waterjet and plasma parts from the DXF: cut length and pierces at your own cut speeds, bends, parts per sheet from the nest, and the finish.
- Quoting from STEP files: Upload a STEP file: the size of the solid sets the blank, and its holes pre-fill drilling, tapping and peck time at your own feeds and seconds per hole.
- Repeat parts and routings: See every earlier quote of a part number, start a repeat from the last won quote's inputs at today's rates, and reuse saved routings by part family.
- Material price tracking: Date every material price, keep its history, import a supplier's price sheet, price bar stock by the foot, and see which open quotes a price change affects.
- Online quote acceptance: Email the quote PDF from the estimator's send button with a link where the customer picks a quantity, adds a PO number and accepts or declines.
- Quote follow-up: Every sent quote gets a follow-up day. A morning email lists each estimator's quotes due, and the quote log keeps every call, so no quote goes quiet.
- Win/loss tracking: See your win rate by customer, material, machine, markup, estimator, routing and month, the reasons you lose, and the unit prices you won and lost at.
- Job travelers: Print a job traveler from a won quote: material and stock to pull, every operation with setup, cycle and run time, finishing, inspection and sign-off lines.
- Shop load and lead time: Put your open jobs on your machines, see the day each one finishes and each machine is booked until, and quote a lead time behind the backlog.

### What it will not do

- Make up a dimension, tolerance, material or quantity that isn't on the drawing or in the email
- Price anything with a rate you didn't set
- Send anything to your customers
- Use your drawings, rates or quotes to train AI models
- Share one shop's rates or drawings with another shop

Defense work: see CUI and export-controlled drawings before sending any.

### How these prices were set

Each plan is priced from what it costs us to run: the AI reading each drawing and checking
itself, hosting and storing drawings, payment fees, a refund reserve and support time, for a shop
that uses its whole allowance. The price is that cost plus a margin of roughly one and a half to two
and a half times, and RFQ allowances are set so no plan sells below that.

#### What counts as an RFQ

One customer request, with any number of parts, up to 10 drawing pages. Bigger packages count once
per 10 pages. Re-reading, editing and re-pricing the same RFQ doesn't count again.

#### Shops on the free plan

We'll tell you about any price change before anything is charged, and nobody is moved
onto a paid plan without choosing it.

## For CMMC-conscious shops

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/for-cmmc-shops

For defense and CMMC-conscious shops

## Quoting help, without putting controlled drawings at risk

Many machine shops quote for defense primes and their suppliers. If some of your RFQs
carry Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) or export-controlled technical data, here is exactly
where Job Shop Quote stands.

### During early access: don't send CUI or ITAR/EAR drawings

Job Shop Quote early access is not set up to hold CUI or export-controlled technical data. Contractors
that store covered defense information with a cloud service are expected to use one that meets
security requirements equivalent to the FedRAMP Moderate baseline
(DFARS 252.204-7012),
and export-controlled drawings have their own rules. We don't claim either, so please use early
access only for commercial RFQs and drawings with no CUI or export-control markings.

If you're not sure whether a drawing is controlled, treat it as controlled and leave it out. Signing up asks for your name, email and shop, never for drawings.

### Why we're building for these shops anyway

CMMC requirements started appearing in Department of Defense contracts on 10 November 2025
(MeriTalk);
check the current rollout schedule for what applies to your contracts. The shops that quote defense
work are often the same small CNC and fabrication shops that Job Shop Quote is for, and they need the
paperwork side handled too.

### Also from us: a CMMC workspace for small shops

Alongside Job Shop Quote we make a separate workspace for CMMC Level 1 and Level 2
self-assessments: the System Security Plan, the plan of action and milestones, and the SPRS score
across the NIST SP 800-171 controls. It is open on a free Level 1 plan. It does not certify anyone
(only an authorized assessor can), and your assessment stays yours to make and sign.

About CMMC Workspace

Want to hear when either is ready for controlled work? Email hello@marisstella.app.

## Machine shop quoting software, compared honestly

Most CNC and fabrication shops quote in one of three ways: a spreadsheet, the quoting
module of their ERP, or dedicated quoting software. Here is what each
costs where a price is published, what it is good at, and where Job Shop Quote fits, including what it
does not do.

### The options side by side

Prices as listed by the source named, on the date given. Vendors change
prices and most quote by shop size, so check with the vendor before you decide.

Your own Excel or Google Sheets workbook

One estimator, a handful of RFQs a week, and a workbook only they need to understand.

Shops that want quoting help without an ERP project, and want to try it on real RFQs before paying anything.

### What Job Shop Quote does today

- Prices each part from the machines, rates, materials, minimums and markups on your rate card.
The math is plain arithmetic you can check line by line; no model sets a price.

- Measures CAD files: a STEP or IGES solid's blank size and hole locations (for roughing and
drilling time at your machine's rates), an STL's size and volume, and a DXF flat pattern's cut
length, pierces and bend lines (for laser, waterjet, plasma and press-brake time, and parts per
sheet).

- Imports your rate card and your supplier's price list from a spreadsheet.

- Builds the quote PDF, emails it when your estimator sends it, keeps revisions, and logs each
quote as won or lost so you can see your win rate by estimator, routing, part family and month.

### What it does not do

- It is not an ERP: no scheduling, work orders, inventory, shop-floor tracking or quality records.
If you need those, JobBOSS² or ProShop are built for it.

- Reading RFQ emails and PDF drawings with AI is built but not switched on in the hosted app yet. Until it is, the app reads them by fixed rules: labelled lines (Part number, Qty, Material, Finish, Due) and parts tables with a header row, each value shown with the line it came from. You check those and enter the rest yourself.

- No connection to an ERP yet. A QuickBooks Online connection is built and switches on once Intuit
approves it.

- Not for CUI or export-controlled drawings during early access (why).

- It is new. The products above have years of shops behind them; Job Shop Quote does not yet, and we
won't pretend otherwise.

### How to choose

- Count your RFQs. A few a week rarely justifies more than a good spreadsheet.
Dozens a week, with parts that repeat, is where quoting software pays for the estimator's time.

- Decide whether you need an ERP. If you already run one, try its quoting module
first. If you don't, buying an ERP just to quote is a large project; quoting-only tools are smaller.

- Know your rates first. Every tool prices from your hourly rates, so a rate that
is too low gives a wrong quote in all of them (how to work one out).

- Price it on your own work. Quote last month's RFQs in any tool you trial and compare
the numbers with what you actually charged and what the jobs cost.

- Check who owns your data. Ask whether your drawings are used to train AI models and
whether you can export your rate card and quote history. (Job Shop Quote: never used for training,
and your rate card exports as a spreadsheet.)

Product names belong to their owners. Maris Stella Labs LLC is not affiliated with any of them.

hello@marisstella.app if one is wrong and we will fix it.

## Machine shop hourly rate

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/machine-shop-hourly-rate

Guide

## How to work out a machine shop hourly rate

The hourly rate on a quote has to pay for the machine, the operator, the building and a
profit, out of the hours a customer actually pays for. Here is a method that starts from your own
books, a worked example, and the mistakes that make a rate too low.

### The method in five steps

- What the machine costs you each year. Take the installed price, subtract what you
expect to sell it for, and divide by the years you will run it. Add a year of maintenance, tooling,
coolant and power for that machine. If you financed it, the interest belongs here too. Power is
hours run × average draw in kW (well under the nameplate) × your price per kWh; the US average
commercial price was 14.27¢ in September 2026
(EIA Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.6.A,
read 2026-11-27), and states differ a lot, so use your own bill.

- Its share of overhead. Rent, insurance, utilities, the office, the estimator, software
and everything else that does not belong to one machine, split across your machines. Splitting by
floor space or by the hours each runs is fairer than an even split when machines differ a lot.

- Billable hours, honestly counted. Not the hours the doors are open: the hours the
machine spends on work a customer pays for. Setups you don't charge, maintenance, prove-outs, scrap
remakes and idle time all come out. Your job records are the best source; a guess here moves the
rate more than any other number.

- The operator. Wage plus payroll taxes, workers' comp, insurance and benefits gives
the cost of a paid hour. The employer's Social Security and Medicare alone are
7.65% of wages (IRS Topic no. 751,
read 2026-11-27); your payroll reports give the rest as a percentage. The operator is paid for more hours than the machine bills, so spread the
whole paid year over the billable hours. One operator tending two machines splits that cost between them.

- Add the profit. Divide the cost of a billable hour by one minus your margin. A 20%
margin means dividing by 0.8, which is not the same as adding 20%.

### A worked example

One 3-axis mill, one operator, one shift. Every number here is made up to show the
arithmetic; they are not typical figures for any region or trade. Use your own.

Made-up shop: 2,000 paid operator hours, of which the mill bills 1,300 (65%).
LineWorked out asAmount

Machine ownership($180,000 − $40,000 resale) ÷ 10 years$14,000 a yearRunning the machinemaintenance, tooling, coolant, power$12,000 a yearIts share of overheadrent, insurance, office, software$30,000 a yearMachine and overhead$56,000 ÷ 1,300 billable hours$43.08 an hourOperator, per paid hour$28.00 wage + 30% taxes, insurance and benefits$36.40 an hourOperator, per billable hour$36.40 × 2,000 paid ÷ 1,300 billable$56.00 an hourCost of a billable hourmachine and overhead + operator$99.08 an hourRate at a 20% margin$99.08 ÷ (1 − 0.2)$123.85 an hour

Two variations on the same shop show which inputs matter most:

- If the operator tends two such mills, each mill carries half the operator and its cost falls from
$99.08 to $71.08 an hour.

- Divide by every paid hour instead of billable hours (the common shortcut of about 2,000 hours a
year) and the cost comes out at $64.40 an hour: $34.68 an hour short, on every hour you bill.

### Utilization moves the rate most

The same made-up mill and costs, billing more or fewer of the operator's 2,000 paid hours:

Only billable hours change; the margin stays 20%.
Billable hoursUtilizationCost an hourRate at 20% margin

1,80090%$71.56$89.441,60080%$80.50$100.631,300 (the example)65%$99.08$123.851,00050%$128.80$161.0080040%$161.00$201.25

Almost every cost is fixed for the year, so each hour you cannot bill is paid for by the hours you
can. A rate set for a busy year loses money in a slow one; set it on the utilization your job records
show, and rework it when the backlog changes.

### Mistakes that make a rate too low

- Counting open hours as billable. The step above: the rate is only as good as the
billable-hours figure, so check it against last year's jobs.

- One rate for every machine. A 5-axis machine and a manual lathe cost very different
amounts to own. A blended rate overprices the simple work you lose and underprices the complex work
you win.

- Mixing up margin and markup. In the example a 20% markup gives
$118.89 an hour, a 20% margin $123.85. Decide which one your
targets mean.

- Leaving setup in the hourly rate. Setup time is real machine time. Charging it as its
own line, or at its own rate, keeps small runs from being priced like large ones.

- Never revisiting it. Wages, rent and power change. Rework the rate when they do,
and at least once a year.

### Where the rate goes next

A rate is half of a quote; the other half is how long the part takes
(how to quote a machining job,
with this rate in a worked example). In Job Shop Quote each machine
on your rate card has its own hourly rate and, if you want one, a separate setup rate. A quote line is
then the time on each machine at that machine's rate, plus material, outside processes, minimums and
your markup, with every figure showing the rate it used. You can
see how a quote is built or import your
existing rate sheet from a spreadsheet.

This page explains a common costing method. It is not accounting, tax or financial
advice; your accountant can tell you how depreciation, financing and overhead are treated in your own
books, and those may differ from the simple straight-line figures used here.

## How to quote a CNC machining job

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/how-to-quote-cnc-machining

Guide

## How to quote a CNC machining job

A machining quote is a handful of numbers added up the same way every time: material,
setup, run time, outside processes and your markup, priced at each quantity the customer asks for.
Here is the method, a worked example at 1, 10 and 100 parts, and the mistakes that lose money on jobs
you win.

### The method in six steps

- Read the RFQ for what changes the price. Material and temper, quantities,
tolerances tighter than your usual, finishes and platings, certifications, inspection reports and the
delivery date. Anything missing is a question to the customer, not a guess.

- Price the material from the blank, not the part. Size the stock you will
actually cut: the part's envelope plus facing and clamping allowance, rounded to a size you can buy.
Weight times price per pound, plus a share for saw kerf and drop, or the price of a whole bar or
plate when that is how you buy it. Keep the supplier's minimum charge.

- List the operations and time each one. For each setup, the minutes to load the
program, set work offsets, touch off tools and run a first article; for each part, the cycle time
plus loading and deburring. Programming is real time too: count it once per job as a setup-only
operation.

- Price time at that machine's rate. Setup minutes ÷ 60 × rate once per lot, cycle
minutes ÷ 60 × rate for every part started. A rate built from your own costs is the foundation
(how to work one out).

- Add outside processes with their lot minimums. Anodize, plating, heat treat and
passivation vendors usually charge per part with a minimum per batch, and for small lots the minimum
is the price.

- Plan for scrap, add markup, and quote every quantity. Start enough parts to ship
the order good, add your markup on material and purchased services, apply a minimum per line, and
repeat the whole sum at each quantity break, since setup and minimums spread differently at each.

### A worked example

A mounting bracket in 6061-T6 aluminum plate, two milling setups and a deburr, anodized by a vendor.
Every number here is made up to show the arithmetic; they are not typical prices,
times or rates for any region or trade. Use your own.

- Blank: 4.25 × 3.25 × 1 in
at 0.0975 lb/in³ = 1.35 lb, at $5.00
a pound plus 10% for kerf and facing, with a $25.00
minimum.

- Time on the 3-axis mill at $123.85 an hour (the rate the
hourly rate guide works out,
profit included, so labor carries no further markup):

- Program and first-article check: 60 min setup, 0 min per part
- Op 1: face, profile, pockets: 45 min setup, 14 min per part
- Op 2: flip, face to thickness, drill and tap: 30 min setup, 8 min per part
- Deburr and inspect: 0 min setup, 4 min per part

135 setup minutes for the lot and 26 minutes per part.

- Clear anodize (outside vendor): $3.50 a part, minimum
$150.00 a lot.

- Fallout: 3% of parts started are expected to scrap, so
each lot starts enough to ship the order good.

- Markup: 15% on material and on the outside service;
a $250.00 minimum per line.

The made-up bracket at three quantities. Each component is rounded to the cent, then summed; the price each is rounded up to the cent.
Line1 part10 parts100 parts

Parts started211104Material$25.00$81.48$770.32Setup$278.67$278.67$278.67Run time$107.34$590.35$5,581.51Anodize (outside)$150.00$150.00$364.00Cost$561.01$1,100.50$6,994.50Markup$26.25$34.72$170.15Price each$587.26$113.53$71.65Line total$587.26$1,135.30$7,165.00

What the table shows:

- Setup is the price of a small order. The same $278.67 of
setup is 47% of the price of one part, 25% at ten and 4%
at a hundred. That is why the price each falls from $587.26 to
$113.53 to $71.65.

- Minimums decide the small lots. At one and ten parts the anodizer's
$150.00 lot minimum is the whole finishing charge, and one part's
material is the $25.00 minimum, not the few dollars the metal weighs.

- Fallout is not free on small lots. At 3% expected fallout,
shipping one good part means starting 2, and shipping a hundred means starting
104. Leave fallout out and the hundred-part line comes to
$6,900.00 instead of $7,165.00:
$265.00 you would otherwise pay for yourself
when the scrap happens.

### Mistakes that lose money on jobs you win

- Pricing from the finished part. The customer pays for the blank you cut, not the
metal left in the part. Price the stock size you will buy.

- Folding setup into the run rate. A per-part price that hides setup is right at one
quantity only. Price setup once per lot and the breaks work out by themselves.

- Forgetting the time that isn't cutting. Programming, first-article inspection,
deburring, part marking and paperwork take machine or operator time on every job.

- Quoting a reorder at the first order's price. A repeat job with a proven program
and fixtures has less setup; a reorder at a smaller quantity may need a higher price each, not the old one.

- No record of how the price was built. When a customer asks why the price changed,
or a job loses money, the basis of every figure is what lets you answer. Keep it with the quote.

- Never comparing quotes with actual jobs. Check the estimated hours against the
traveler on jobs you win. Times that are always short are a rate problem in disguise.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

Job Shop Quote prices a quote line exactly this way. Your rate card holds each machine's hourly rate
(and a setup rate if you use one), your materials by the pound, by the foot or by the stock piece,
your finishing and outside services with their lot minimums, your markups and line minimum. The
estimator enters the blank, the operations and their times, and the quantity breaks; the price at each
break follows, every figure showing the rate it came from, and a line missing a time or a material is
blocked rather than priced as if it were free. The example above is priced to the cent the app gives
for the same inputs, checked by a test in its code. You can
see how a quote is built or
compare it with other quoting software. Laser,
plasma or press-brake work: see how to
quote sheet metal and laser cut parts; welded frames and fabrications:
how to quote welding jobs. What to put on the quote you send, with a template to
download: machine shop quote
template.

This page explains a common costing method. It is not accounting, tax or
financial advice, and the prices, times and rates in it are made up. Check every quote before you send
it.

## How to quote sheet metal and laser cut parts

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/how-to-quote-sheet-metal

Guide

## How to quote sheet metal and laser cut parts

A sheet-metal quote comes from the flat pattern: how long the cut path is, how many
times the head pierces, how many bends, and how many parts nest on a sheet you buy whole. Here is the
method, a worked example at 10, 100 and 500 parts, and the
mistakes that lose money on jobs you win.

### The method in six steps

- Read the RFQ for what changes the price. Material, gauge and finish,
quantities, hardware to insert, weld or powder-coat requirements, flatness and tolerance callouts,
certifications and the delivery date. A missing gauge or grade is a question to the customer, not a
guess.

- Measure the flat pattern. From the DXF: the blank's overall size, the total
cut length (outline plus every hole and slot), the number of pierces (one per closed contour) and the
bend lines. A STEP model of a bent part has to be unfolded first; quote from the flat.

- Nest the blank and count sheets. How many blanks fit on the sheet size you
stock at the gap your material needs. Material is the number of sheets the lot uses, bought whole,
unless you have a real use for the remnant.

- Time the cut at your own speed for that material and gauge. Cut minutes = cut
length ÷ cutting speed, plus pierces × pierce time. Cutting speed changes several-fold with alloy
and thickness, so one speed per machine is wrong for most parts; use your machine's cut chart.

- Time the bends and the rest. Seconds per bend times the bends, a brake setup
per lot, programming and nesting once per job, deburring and inspection per part, each at that
machine's or bench's own rate.

- Add outside processes, plan for scrap, add markup and quote every quantity.
Powder coat and plating carry lot minimums; start enough parts to ship the order good; repeat the
sum at each break, since sheets, setups and minimums spread differently at each.

### A worked example

A mounting bracket in 14 ga (0.075 in) cold-rolled steel, laser cut, bent twice, deburred and powder coated by a vendor.
Every number here is made up to show the arithmetic; they are not typical speeds,
prices or rates for any machine, region or trade. Use your own.

- Flat pattern (from the DXF): 6.3 × 9.1 in overall,
41.8 in of cut path, 7 pierces (the outline and six holes),
2 bend lines. Rounded up to the next 1/8 in, the blank is 6.375 ×
9.125 in.

- Material: 48 × 120 in sheet at $98.00 a sheet. A
rectangular nest at a 0.25 in gap fits 90 blanks a sheet.

- Fiber laser at $165.00 an hour:
160 in/min in this gauge and 0.8 s a pierce, so
41.8 ÷ 160 + 7 × 0.8
s = 0.355 min, rounded up to 0.36 min a part;
15 min to load the sheet program, plus a one-time
30 min to program and nest the job.

- Press brake at $95.00 an hour:
2 bends × 9 s = 0.30 min a part,
20 min to set up the tooling and back gauge.

- Bench at
$65.00 an hour: deburr and inspect,
0.75 min a part.

- Black powder coat (outside vendor): $2.75 a part, minimum
$175.00 a lot.

- Fallout: 2% of parts started are expected to scrap.

- Markup: 20% on material,
15% on the outside service, none on labor (the machine rates are
taken to hold the margin already); a $150.00 minimum per line.

The made-up bracket at three quantities. Each component is rounded to the cent, then summed; the price each is rounded up to the cent.
Line10 parts100 parts500 parts

Parts started11103511Sheets126Material$98.00$196.00$588.00Setup and programming$155.42$155.42$155.42Run time$25.06$234.59$1,163.81Powder coat (outside)$175.00$283.25$1,405.25Cost$453.48$869.26$3,312.48Markup$45.85$81.69$328.39Price each$49.94$9.51$7.29Line total$499.40$951.00$3,645.00

What the table shows:

- Small lots buy a whole sheet. 11 parts need one sheet that holds
90: the $98.00 sheet is the material charge whether you
cut 11 blanks or 90. At 500 parts the same material is
6 sheets, and the last one carries only 61 parts.

- The vendor's minimum decides the small lot. At 10 parts the powder
coater's $175.00 lot minimum is
39% of the cost; at 500 the
per-part charge has long passed it.

- Fixed charges spread out. The same $155.42 of setup and
programming, the first sheet and the coater's minimum are shared by 10,
100 or 500 parts. Together they are why the price each falls from
$49.94 to $9.51 to
$7.29, while the run time per part stays the same.

- Laser time is short; it still adds up. 0.36 min a part is
$0.99 at
this rate. Leave out the pierces and the cut drops to
0.261 min; on thick plate, where a pierce
takes seconds, the pierces can be most of the cut.

### Mistakes that lose money on jobs you win

- Pricing material by the part's area. You buy sheets. Unless the skeleton and
remnant really go back on the rack and get used, the lot pays for the sheets it consumes.

- One cutting speed for everything. A speed from thin mild steel will badly
under-time stainless or thick plate. Keep speeds per material and gauge.

- Forgetting pierces. A part with many small holes can spend more time piercing
than cutting, especially in thicker material.

- Leaving out programming and nesting. It is real time on every new part number,
once per job, not per part.

- Ignoring the brake setup. A new tool change and back-gauge setup is the same on
ten parts or a thousand; price it once per lot.

- Quoting from a 3D model nobody unfolded. The flat pattern sets the blank, the cut
length and the bends; check the bend allowance your brake actually gives.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

Job Shop Quote reads an ASCII DXF flat pattern attached to the RFQ by fixed rules in its own code,
with no AI involved: the overall size, the cut length, the pierces and the bend lines drawn on a layer
named for bends. On your rate card each machine can carry a cutting speed, a pierce time and seconds
per bend, and a cutting machine can carry its own speed per material and gauge (typed, or imported
from your cut chart as a spreadsheet). A quote line then starts with a "Cut from DXF" and a "Bend from
DXF" operation timed exactly as above, a blank sized from the flat pattern and, for a material you buy
by the sheet, the parts per sheet from a rectangular nest at your gap. Every figure shows the rate it
came from, the estimator can change any of them, and nothing is suggested when the drawing was read
with low confidence or two machines could run the job. The example above is priced to the cent the
app gives for the same inputs, checked by a test in its code.

No account needed to try the arithmetic: the free
DXF nesting tool nests your parts in the
browser and prices the nest from your rates. For machined parts, see
how to quote a CNC machining job;
for welded assemblies, how to quote
welding and fabrication jobs; for what goes on the quote you send, the
machine shop quote template.

This page explains a common costing method. It is not accounting, tax or
financial advice, and the speeds, prices, times and rates in it are made up. Check every quote before
you send it.

## How to quote welding and fabrication jobs

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/how-to-quote-welding

Guide

## How to quote welding and fabrication jobs

A weldment quote is mostly time: cutting and fitting the pieces, building the fixture,
and the welder's hours, of which the arc is lit for only part. Here is the method, a worked example at
1, 10 and 50 frames, and the mistakes that lose money on
jobs you win.

### The method in six steps

- Read the drawing for what changes the price. Material and section sizes, every
weld symbol (type, size, length, all-around), the process and any welding code or procedure it
calls for, welder qualifications, weld inspection or testing, flatness and finish. A missing weld size
or code is a question to the customer, not a guess.

- Make the cut list. Each piece, its length, end cuts (square, miter, cope) and
section. Add the lengths per section and allow for kerf, squaring cuts and the drop at the end of
each stick.

- Add up the weld. Total inches of each weld size from the symbols. Arc minutes =
weld length ÷ travel speed for that size, position and process.

- Turn arc time into welder time. Welder minutes = arc minutes ÷ operator factor,
the share of the welder's time with the arc lit. The rest is positioning, changing angles, cleaning
between passes and moving the part; use the figure you measure in your own shop.

- Price fit-up, the fixture and the rest. Fitting and tacking per part, building
the fixture once per job, saw cuts per piece, grinding, cleaning and inspection per part, each at
that station's own rate. Add the filler wire (from the weld metal, at your deposition efficiency)
and shielding gas.

- Add outside processes, markup and quote every quantity. Galvanizing, powder
coat and paint carry lot minimums; repeat the sum at each break, since the fixture, the first
article and the coater's minimum spread differently at each.

### A worked example

A steel cart frame: 8 pieces of 2 × 2 × 1/8 in square tube, sawn, fitted and tacked in
a fixture, MIG welded, ground and powder coated by a vendor. Every number here is made up to
show the arithmetic; they are not typical speeds, prices, rates or operator factors for any
process, region or trade. Use your own.

- Material: 8 pieces, 216 in of tube
(18 ft) a frame, at $4.50 a foot plus
10% for kerf, squaring and drop: $89.10 a frame.

- Band saw at $75.00 an hour:
8 cuts × 1.5 min = 12 min a frame (load, measure,
cut, deburr the end), 15 min to set the stop and the miter.

- Fixture, fit and tack in the MIG welding cell at
$95.00 an hour: 90 min to build the fixture once for
the job, 12 min a frame to load, square and tack.

- Weld out: 64 in of 3/16 in
fillet at 10 in/min is 6.40 arc minutes. At a
35% operator factor the welder spends 6.40 ÷
0.35 = 18.286 min, rounded up to
18.29 min a frame.

- Bench at $65.00 an hour:
grind, clean and inspect, 10 min a frame; a
30 min first-article check once per job.

- Wire and gas: a 3/16 in fillet
is a triangle of 0.0176 sq in, so 64 in of it is
0.319 lb of steel at 0.284 lb/cu in. At
90% deposition efficiency that is 0.355 lb of wire
at $3.50 a lb ($1.24), plus
35 cu ft/h of gas for 6.40 arc minutes, 3.73 cu ft at
$0.12 ($0.45): $1.69
a frame.

- Black powder coat (outside vendor): $35.00 a frame, minimum
$225.00 a lot.

- Markup: 20% on material and consumables,
15% on the outside service, none on labor (the shop rates are taken
to hold the margin already); a $250.00 minimum per line.

The made-up cart frame at three quantities. Each component is rounded to the cent, then summed; the price each is rounded up to the cent.
Line1 frame10 frames50 frames

Material (tube)$89.10$891.00$4,455.00Setup, fixture and first article$193.75$193.75$193.75Run time$73.79$737.92$3,689.63Wire and gas$1.69$16.90$84.50Powder coat (outside)$225.00$350.00$1,750.00Cost$583.33$2,189.57$10,172.88Markup$51.91$234.08$1,170.40Price each$635.24$242.37$226.87Line total$635.24$2,423.70$11,343.50

What the table shows:

- The operator factor is the biggest single assumption. Priced on arc time alone,
the weld would be $10.13 a frame; priced on the welder's time it is
$28.96. Guess the factor high and every frame you win loses the difference.

- Consumables are small next to labor. Wire and gas are $1.69
a frame against $28.96 of welding. A price built up from pounds of wire misses
most of the cost.

- The fixture and the coater's minimum decide the one-off. At
1 frame the $193.75 of fixture, saw setup and first article and
the $225.00 coating minimum are
72% of the cost. At
50 the same setups are $3.88 a frame.
That is why the price each falls from $635.24 to
$242.37 to $226.87.

- At volume it is run time and tube. At 50 frames, run time
($3,689.63) and tube ($4,455.00) are
80% of the cost; a
faster fixture or a better cut list is where a lower price would come from.

### Mistakes that lose money on jobs you win

- Pricing weld by arc time. The welder is paid for every minute, not just the
ones with the arc lit. Measure your operator factor on real jobs and use it.

- One travel speed for every weld. Weld size, position, process and the number of
passes change it several-fold; a vertical or overhead weld or a multi-pass fillet is far slower than
a flat single pass.

- Leaving out fit-up and tacking. On small weldments it can take as long as the
welding.

- Forgetting the fixture. It is real time once per job, and it is the reason a
one-off costs so much more than the tenth piece.

- Leaving out grinding, cleanup and distortion. Weld spatter, blending and
straightening a frame that pulled out of square all take time per part.

- Missing a code or inspection callout. A welding procedure, qualified welders,
or visual, dye-penetrant or other testing called out on the drawing add time and paperwork that the
weld length alone does not show.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

Job Shop Quote does not read weld symbols or measure weld length: you work out the times above and
type them in. Each quote line then carries the tube from your rate card priced by the foot (the
frame's total length as the blank length, kerf and drop as the row's scrap allowance), one operation
per station at that machine's rate (saw, fit and tack, weld, grind), the fixture as a setup that is
charged once per quantity break, wire and gas as an extra per part, and the powder coat as an
outside service with its lot minimum. Every quantity break then follows, every figure showing the rate
it came from, and a line missing a time or a material is blocked rather than priced as if it were
free. The example above is priced to the cent the app gives for the same inputs, checked by a test in
its code. You can see how a quote is built.

For your shop rate itself, see how
to work out a machine shop hourly rate. Laser-cut and bent parts:
how to quote sheet metal;
machined parts: how to quote a CNC
machining job; what goes on the quote you send: the
machine shop quote template.

This page explains a common costing method. It is not accounting, tax,
engineering or financial advice, does not say what a welding code requires, and the speeds, factors,
prices, times and rates in it are made up. Check every quote before you send it.

## Machine shop quote template

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/machine-shop-quote-template

Guide

## Machine shop quote template

What a CNC or fabrication quote needs on it, what to keep off it, the terms to decide
once, a filled-in example and a free template to download. The buyer reads a quote to compare it with
two others and to write a purchase order from it; every field below serves one of those.

Download the template (CSV)

### What goes on a machine shop quote

FieldWhy it is there

Your shop's name, address, phone and emailSo the buyer can reach the person who quoted, and a purchase order goes to the right place.Quote number and revisionOne number per quote, and a revision label when you re-quote, so a PO names exactly which prices it accepts.Date and valid-until dateMaterial and machine time get repriced; a quote without an end date can be held against you a year later.Customer company, contact and their RFQ numberBuyers send many RFQs; their reference is how they match your quote to theirs.Part number and drawing revision for every lineThe price is for that revision. When the drawing changes, the revision on your quote shows which one you priced.Description: material, finish and anything else priced inThe buyer compares quotes line by line; saying “6061-T6, clear anodize, certs included” stops a cheaper quote that left them out looking like the same thing.Every quantity asked for, with unit and extended priceSetup and lot minimums spread differently at each quantity, so each break gets its own price, not one price each.Lead time, counted from the order“3 weeks after receipt of order” holds; a calendar date goes stale while the buyer decides.Notes: assumptions and exceptionsAnything you assumed (a tolerance, a material substitute, an inspection level) written down before the PO, not argued about after.TermsPayment, shipping, overruns and the rest, decided once and printed on every quote (list below).

### What stays off it

Your cost basis. The customer sees a price for each part at each quantity; your hourly rates, setup
and cycle minutes, material cost and markup stay in your own records. A quote that shows them invites
the buyer to negotiate each one, and tells a competitor your rates. Keep the basis with the quote on
your side, so you can answer when a reorder is priced differently
(how a machining price is built).

### A filled-in example

The shop, customer, part, dates and prices are made up. The prices are the worked
example in how to quote a CNC
machining job, priced at three quantities.

Example Precision Machining: quote Q-1001, dated 2026-11-27, valid until
2026-12-27. Prepared for Example Customer Co., A. Buyer, purchasing. Lead time: 3 weeks after receipt of order.
PartQtyUnit priceExtended

BRK-1001 Rev BMounting bracket, per drawing BRK-1001 Rev B. 6061-T6 aluminum, clear anodize (outside vendor).1$587.26$587.2610$113.53$1,135.30100$71.65$7,165.00

Notes

- Quoted to drawing BRK-1001 Rev B dated 2026-11-20. A later revision is a new quote.
- Material certifications included. First-article inspection report included on the first lot.
- Customer RFQ 2291.

### Terms to decide once

Each of these is a question your terms should answer. Decide them for your shop, put them in one
paragraph and print it on every quote. They are prompts, not wording to copy: have your own terms
and conditions reviewed by someone qualified where you do business.

- Validity. How many days the prices hold, and what happens after: a re-quote, or prices adjusted for material.
- Payment. Net 30 or another term, a deposit on large or first orders, and whether you take cards.
- Drawing revision. That the price is for the revision quoted, and a change to the drawing is a new quote or a change order.
- Overruns and underruns. Whether you may ship a few parts over or under the order quantity, and how those are billed.
- Inspection and paperwork. Which certifications, first-article or CMM reports are included, and which are charged extra.
- Shipping. Where ownership and risk pass (FOB your dock or theirs, or an Incoterm), and who pays freight.
- Customer-supplied material. Who carries the cost when material or parts the customer supplied scrap through no fault of yours.
- Changes and cancellation. What the customer owes for material bought and work done when an order is changed or cancelled.
- Export-controlled drawings. Whether you accept ITAR or EAR technical data, and how the customer must mark and send it.

### The template

machine-shop-quote-template.csv opens in Excel,
Google Sheets or LibreOffice. It has the columns Line, Part number, Drawing revision, Description, Material, Finish, Quantity, Unit price, Extended price, Lead time, Notes: one row per quantity
break, so a part quoted at three quantities takes three rows with the same line number. The example
rows are marked; delete them. It holds plain values, no formulas: work out the extended price as
quantity × unit price, and put your shop's header, the customer, the dates and your terms above the
table when you print it.

A spreadsheet works for a few quotes a week. It stops working when you need to find what you quoted
a part at last time, re-quote a revision, see which quotes are about to expire or remember to follow up.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

Job Shop Quote builds this quote as a PDF from your rate card: your shop's name, logo and contact
lines, a quote number with revisions (“Q-1001 Rev 2, replaces Q-1001”), the date, a valid-until
date from your default number of days, the customer, a lead time from your default, every part with its
revision and description, a row per quantity break with unit and extended prices, the quote's notes and
your terms, saved once in the rate card. It never prints your rates, times or markup. The estimator
checks and sends it; the customer gets a link to accept or decline, and the app reminds you about
follow-ups and quotes about to expire. You can
see how a quote is built.

This page describes common practice for job-shop quotes. It is not legal, tax or
financial advice, and the example's names, dates and prices are made up. Check every quote before you
send it.

## FAQ

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/faq

FAQ

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I use Job Shop Quote today?

Yes. Sign up free at https://jobshop-quote.marisstella.app/sign-up. The Early access plan covers up to 40 RFQs a month for 3 people, with no card. It prices the parts you enter, and what it measures from STEP, IGES, STL and DXF files, from your rate card, builds the quote PDF, emails it when your estimator sends it, and keeps the won/lost log. Reading RFQ emails and PDF drawings with AI is built but not switched on in the hosted app yet. Until it is, the app reads them by fixed rules: labelled lines (Part number, Qty, Material, Finish, Due) and parts tables with a header row, each value shown with the line it came from. You check those and enter the rest yourself.

### Does the AI decide my prices?

No. Prices come only from the rates, minimums and markups you set. The AI reads the RFQ and drawings and proposes setups and cycle times with its reasoning shown; your estimator accepts or corrects them, and the dollar math is plain arithmetic on your rate table.

### How does it price material: by weight, by the bar or by the foot?

Whichever way you buy it. Each material on your rate table is priced by weight (your price per lb or per cwt and density, plus scrap), by the stock piece (a sheet or a cut blank), or by length for bar, tube and extrusion: your price per foot or per metre, a cut allowance for kerf and facing, and, if you buy in fixed bars, the bar length and remnant, so a line is charged the whole bars its parts need. You can import these from your supplier's price list as a spreadsheet: before you save, each row shows its price change and the open quotes priced at the old price, and the supplier and the list's date are kept in each price's history. A price per cwt or per metre is kept exactly as your supplier quotes it, so $412.50/cwt prices at $4.125/lb, not a rounded $4.13.

### What does it read?

The STEP, IGES, STL and DXF measurements work today; reading email text and PDF drawings with AI is not switched on in the hosted app yet. RFQ email text and PDF drawings, including scans, plus STEP and DXF files. A STEP solid gives the blank size and, with your machine's measured removal rate, a roughing time; with your seconds per hole and, if you enter one, your drill feed for each hole's depth, a drilling time that counts a counterbored hole once, flags holes deeper than 3× their diameter and leaves bores over 1 in to you; tick which hole sizes are threaded and, with your seconds per tapped hole, it adds a tapping time. A DXF flat pattern gives a laser, waterjet or plasma cutting time from its cut length and pierces at your cut speed (one per machine, or your own speed for each material and thickness from your cut charts), and a press-brake time from its bend lines; on a material sold by the sheet, with your sheet size and nest gap, it counts how many flat blanks fit on one sheet (a rectangular nest, so a nesting program may fit more, never fewer). An IGES solid gives the blank size and hole locations like a STEP file (no volume: send STEP for that). An STL mesh gives its size and, when closed, its volume; an STL carries no units, so your estimator picks millimetres or inches. Native SolidWorks files are not measured yet.

### What happens when a drawing is unclear?

The value is flagged for your estimator with the drawing page it came from. It is never filled in with a guess.

### Will it send quotes to my customers?

No. Your estimator reviews and approves every quote and sends it themselves: by email from the app, as a PDF, or copied into your own email or ERP.

### Will you use my drawings to train AI models?

No. Your drawings, rates and quotes are used only to quote for your shop. They are never used to train AI models and never shared with another shop.

### Can I send CUI or export-controlled (ITAR/EAR) drawings?

Not during early access: it isn't set up for controlled data. Use it only for commercial RFQs. The page for CMMC-conscious shops explains why.

### Does it connect to my ERP or quoting system?

Not yet in the hosted app: download the quote PDF or copy it across. A QuickBooks Online connection, which turns a won quote into an invoice, is built and switches on once Intuit approves it. Tell us which system you use at hello@marisstella.app; that decides what gets connected next.

### What does it cost?

The Early access plan is free, with no card. Paid plans start at $199 a month, priced from what it costs to run; they are not on sale yet. Nobody is moved onto a paid plan without choosing it.

### Who is building it?

Maris Stella Labs LLC, a small software company that also makes Grant Autopilot for nonprofits.

Something else? Email hello@marisstella.app.

### Try it on your own RFQs

The Early access plan is free and needs no card.

Start free

## CNC quoting software that prices from your own rate card

For the owner or estimator who quotes machined parts today in a spreadsheet or from memory. You enter your machines, materials and outside processes once; each quote line is then priced by plain arithmetic on those rates, with every figure showing the rate it used.

Start free

### What it does

- A rate card of machines (hourly rate, optional setup rate, default setup), materials (per lb with density and scrap, per stock piece or by the foot, with a minimum charge), finishing and outside services (per part with a lot minimum), markups on labor, material and outside work, and a line minimum
- Each line priced at every quantity break from setup, cycle time, material and finishing, with the rates frozen into the quote so later rate changes never move a sent price
- Blocking issues instead of guesses: a line missing a cycle time, a material price or a blank size says so and is not priced
- Import the rate card from your own spreadsheet (.xlsx or CSV, read in the browser), and download it again as one Excel workbook with a tab per kind
- A quote PDF on your letterhead with your logo, showing prices, dates, lead time and terms and none of the costs, rates or markups behind them
- Revisions (Q-1001 Rev 2) with what changed from the last one, side by side, and an optional "Changes from" section on the customer PDF
- A default fallout percentage, so 100 good parts at 3% start 104 without typing it on each line

### What it does not do yet

- Reading RFQ emails and PDF drawings with AI is built but not switched on in the hosted app yet; until it is, labelled lines and parts tables are read by fixed rules and you enter the rest
- Setup and cycle times are yours to enter, or suggested from STEP and DXF measurements at the rates you set; nothing is assumed
- No ERP connection is on yet; the quote is a PDF you download or email

Reading RFQ emails and PDF drawings with AI is built but not switched on in the hosted app yet. Until it is, the app reads them by fixed rules: labelled lines (Part number, Qty, Material, Finish, Due) and parts tables with a header row, each value shown with the line it came from. You check those and enter the rest yourself.

### Free guides on this

- How to quote a CNC machining job
- How to work out a machine shop hourly rate
- Machine shop quote template (free CSV)
- Machine shop quoting software compared

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Where do the prices come from?

Only from your rate card. The same inputs always give the same price, every line lists the rates it used, and a value the app cannot work out stops the line instead of being guessed.

## Sheet metal quoting software

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/sheet-metal-quoting-software

In the app today

## Sheet metal quoting from the DXF flat pattern

For fabrication shops that quote laser-cut, waterjet or plasma parts and press-brake work. Upload the customer's DXF and the quote line starts with the cut, pierce and bend times at your own speeds, and the sheets the order needs from a nest of the flat pattern.

Start free

### What it does

- Cut length, pierces and bend lines measured from an ASCII DXF flat pattern, each with a confidence and flag shown on the RFQ
- "Cut from DXF" and "Bend from DXF" operations pre-filled at the machine's cut speed, pierce seconds and seconds per bend
- Cut speeds per material and thickness from your own cut chart, typed in or imported from a CSV, so a 0.5 in A36 part is timed at that gauge's speed
- The blank from the flat size and the material row's sheet thickness, and parts per sheet from a rectangular nest on the row's sheet width, length and gap
- The same rate card, quantity breaks, finishing and quote PDF as machined parts

### What it does not do yet

- Nesting is rectangular: L-shapes and other odd outlines are not nested by their true shape yet
- A DXF whose outline or holes read with low confidence, or whose bend lines are only dashed, gets no suggestion; you enter the times
- No cut speeds are assumed: with none on your card for the material, the machine's default speed applies, and with none at all nothing is suggested

### Free guides on this

- How to quote sheet metal and laser cut parts
- How to quote welding and fabrication jobs
- How to work out a machine shop hourly rate

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Does it need my cut chart?

It needs the speeds you cut at. Enter a default per machine, or a speed per material and thickness, typed in or imported from the cut chart as a CSV; the quote line names which speed it used.

## Quoting from STEP files

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/step-file-quoting

In the app today

## Quote from the customer's STEP file

For machine shops that get 3D models with their RFQs. The app measures the solid and turns what it finds into suggested operations at the rates you set, each labelled with how it was worked out, for the estimator to accept or change.

Start free

### What it does

- STEP solids measured for size, volume and holes; IGES solids for size and holes; STL meshes for size and volume
- The solid's bounding box pre-fills the blank, and with one machine that has a measured removal rate, a "Rough from CAD" operation
- Hole locations pre-fill "Drill from CAD" at the machine's seconds per hole plus each hole's depth at its drill feed, with counterbores counted once and bores over 1 in left out
- Drill feeds by material, and peck time for holes deeper than 3×D at the machine's peck depth and seconds per peck
- Tapping: the estimator ticks which hole sizes are threaded and the quote adds "Tap from CAD" at the machine's seconds per tapped hole

### What it does not do yet

- Native SolidWorks and other proprietary CAD files are stored but not measured
- One time per tapped hole: tap size and pitch are not timed separately yet
- Only roughing, drilling, tapping and pecking are timed from the model; enter the other operations' times yourself

### Free guides on this

- How to quote a CNC machining job
- How to work out a machine shop hourly rate

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Does it write CAM toolpaths?

No. It measures the model for quoting: the blank, roughing from a removal rate you measured, and drilling, tapping and pecking from the holes. It does not program the part.

### Is Job Shop Quote new?

Yes. It opened in November 2026 and has no customers, reviews or published results yet. What this page describes works in the hosted app today; check every price, time and quantity before you send a quote.

## Repeat parts and routings

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/repeat-part-quoting

In the app today

## Repeat parts quoted from what you quoted before

Most job shops quote the same part numbers again and again. The app shows what you quoted a part at before, what won and what lost, and lets you start the new quote from the last won one, priced from today's rate card.

Start free

### What it does

- "Quoted before: N earlier quotes" on each line and on the RFQ review: quote number, customer, date, status, PO or loss reason, revision, unit price at each break, material and operations
- "Use these inputs" copies an earlier line's cost inputs onto a draft and re-prices it from today's rates
- An optional shop setting pre-fills each new line whose part number and revision match a won quote, labelled "Pre-filled from Q-1001"
- Routings: save a line's operations and finishing as a named routing with a part family, apply or append it on any line, edit it on its own page
- Up to three routings suggested from the line's material and description, each with the evidence it rests on from your own earlier lines

### What it does not do yet

- Routings hold operations and times, never prices: a routing always prices at today's rate card
- Suggestions come only from your shop's own records, so a new shop has none until it has quoted

### Free guides on this

- How to quote a CNC machining job
- Machine shop quote template (free CSV)

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Does a repeat part keep last year's price?

No. It keeps last time's inputs (operations, times, material, blank) and prices them from today's rate card, and the earlier prices are shown beside it so you can see the difference.

## Material price tracking

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/material-price-tracking

In the app today

## Material prices with dates, history and the quotes they change

Metal prices move, and a quote priced off a stale number loses money or loses the job. The app dates every price on your rate card, keeps its history, and shows which open quotes were priced at a price the card no longer has.

Start free

### What it does

- "Price set N days ago" on each material, amber past the shop's limit (90 days by default), and a flag on draft lines that use a stale price
- A price history per material: who set it, when, by how much it moved, and from which supplier's price list and date
- A supplier's price sheet imported from a spreadsheet, with a preview of each price move and the open quotes it touches before anything is saved
- "Quotes this changes": every open quote priced at a price the card no longer has, filtered by how far it moved
- Bar, tube and extrusion priced by the foot, with cut allowance, bar length and remnant, charged in whole bars; prices per cwt and per metre kept exactly

### What it does not do yet

- Nothing re-prices on its own: drafts are re-priced when the estimator presses Re-price, and sent quotes keep the price the customer saw
- Prices come from your rate card and your suppliers' sheets; there is no live metal price feed

### Free guides on this

- How to quote a CNC machining job
- How to quote sheet metal and laser cut parts

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Can I load my supplier's price list?

Yes, as a spreadsheet: the Materials import reads price per lb, per piece, per foot, per cwt or per metre, keeps the supplier and the list's date in each price's history, and shows the moves before you save.

## Online quote acceptance

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/online-quote-acceptance

In the app today

## Quotes your customer can accept online, with a PO number

Once the estimator marks a quote sent, the app emails the exact PDF and can add a link where the customer accepts or declines without an account. An acceptance marks the quote won at the quantity they chose; a decline marks it lost with their reason.

Start free

### What it does

- "Email to customer" sends the PDF frozen at sending (checked against its SHA-256), From your shop, Reply-To the estimator, with the shop's signature
- The customer's link shows the quote as sent and the PDF, never rates, costs or markups; they pick one quoted quantity per part, type a name and an optional PO number and note
- Accepting marks the quote won at the chosen breaks' total with the PO; declining marks it lost with "Declined online" and the reason
- The estimators who made or emailed the quote get the answer by email; links can be turned off at once

### What it does not do yet

- One answer per quote; a quantity the quote does not carry needs a new quote
- No e-signature line on acceptance yet
- The app never sends a quote by itself: an estimator presses send

### Free guides on this

- Machine shop quote template (free CSV)
- How to quote a CNC machining job

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Does my customer need an account?

No. The link opens the quote as it was sent. Only a hash of the link's token is stored, and the link takes no answer past the quote's valid-until day, and stops working when you turn it off.

Yes. It opened in November 2026 and has no customers, reviews or published results yet. What this page describes works in the hosted app today; check every price, time and quantity before you send a quote.

## Quote follow-up

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/quote-follow-up-software

In the app today

## Follow up on every quote you send

A quote that is never followed up is a quote half lost. Sending a quote sets its first follow-up day; the quote log and a morning email tell each estimator which quotes are due, and every call or email is logged on the quote.

Start free

### What it does

- A first follow-up day set when the quote is sent, a number of days after sending that the shop chooses (3 by default; a weekend moves to Monday)
- A "Follow up" card on the quote log: quotes due today, longest overdue first, with contact, total, sent day, valid-until, estimator and the last note
- "Log follow-up" records what happened and the next day: in 1 to 14 days, a date, or no more follow-ups
- One email each morning to each estimator listing their own quotes due, and another listing quotes that expire today or tomorrow
- Quotes expire the day after their valid-until day, and Revise starts the next revision

### What it does not do yet

- The follow-up itself is yours: the app reminds and logs, it does not email the customer for you
- Each member can turn the reminder emails off for themselves

### Free guides on this

- Machine shop quote template (free CSV)
- Machine shop quoting software compared

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Which quotes come up for follow-up?

Sent quotes whose follow-up day has come. Won, lost, expired and replaced quotes never do, and a quote the expiry email already names is left out of the follow-up email.

Yes. It opened in November 2026 and has no customers, reviews or published results yet. What this page describes works in the hosted app today; check every price, time and quantity before you send a quote.

## Win/loss tracking

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/quote-win-rate-tracking

In the app today

## Your quote win rate, and where you win and lose

Mark each quote won (with the PO) or lost (with the reason), or let the customer's online answer do it, and the Win/loss page shows where your prices win, where they lose, and at what price.

Start free

### What it does

- Win rate and won value by customer, material, machine and markup band, over 90 days, 12 months or all time
- Win rate by month and by estimator, by the routing a line was built from, and by part family
- The cost-weighted markup of won against lost quotes, and lost reasons tallied
- "What price did we win at": each part's won and lost quotes with every quantity break's unit price
- A CSV download of the report

### What it does not do yet

- Counted from your own decided quotes only; rows under 5 decided quotes are marked "few"
- Expired quotes are shown but not counted in the win rate

### Free guides on this

- How to work out a machine shop hourly rate
- How to quote a CNC machining job

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### How is the win rate counted?

Won divided by won plus lost, from the quotes your shop marked won or lost (or the customer answered online). Expired quotes are listed but left out of the rate.

## Job travelers

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/job-traveler-software

In the app today

## A job traveler from the quote you won

The estimate already holds the routing, so the floor's copy should not be typed again. Once a quote is won, the app prints a traveler per part from the quote's own operations, with no prices on it.

Start free

### What it does

- One sheet per part: customer, quote, PO and due date; quantity ordered and parts to start at the line's fallout
- The material, its stock description, the blank and the stock pieces or bars to pull, with a cut list for bar stock
- Every operation numbered 10, 20, 30 in the estimate's order with its work center, setup, cycle per part and run time
- Finishing and outside services after them, final inspection, a sign-off line per step and a heat/lot box
- The quantity from the PO you type, or the break the customer accepted online; a multi-break line with neither is refused, never guessed

### What it does not do yet

- A traveler is a PDF to print: there is no saved work order number, status or barcode time tracking yet
- Won quotes only

### Free guides on this

- How to quote a CNC machining job
- How to quote welding and fabrication jobs

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Do prices show on the traveler?

No. It carries quantities, material, operations and times only; no price, rate or markup appears on it.

## Shop load and lead time

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/machine-shop-lead-time

In the app today

## Quote lead times from your real shop load

A lead time typed from habit ("3 weeks ARO") is the one promise a shop most often breaks. The Shop load page puts the open jobs on the machines, and a draft quote's card plans each quantity break behind them.

Start free

### What it does

- Open jobs (won and not shipped) placed on the machines by due date, each operation in the estimate's order at setup plus cycle times the starts
- Each machine's hours a day, Monday to Friday, set by an admin
- Each job's finish day and "after the due date" when it is late; each machine's open hours and the day it is booked until
- On a draft quote, "Lead time from shop load" gives the day, the working days and "N weeks ARO" for every quantity break
- A won quote's Job card saves the due date, the quantity ordered and the shipped day

### What it does not do yet

- Holidays, work already done on a job, finishing and outside-service days are not counted, and the page says so
- A machine with no hours a day or a line with no cycle time is listed as "can't plan" with the reason

### Free guides on this

- How to work out a machine shop hourly rate
- Machine shop quote template (free CSV)

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Is this a full scheduling system?

No. It is a finite-capacity estimate from your quotes' own routings, good enough to quote a date. It does not track work done on the floor or move jobs around for you.

### Is Job Shop Quote new?

Yes. It opened in November 2026 and has no customers, reviews or published results yet. What this page describes works in the hosted app today; check every price, time and quantity before you send a quote.

## Privacy

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/privacy

Privacy

## Site privacy notice

These pages have no forms, set no cookies and load no analytics or third-party
scripts, so they store nothing about you.

### The app has its own policy

When you sign up, Job Shop Quote stores your account, your shop's rates, RFQs, files and quotes. What
it keeps, why and for how long is in its
privacy policy, alongside the
terms of service.

### Hosting

The site is served by Cloudflare, which, like any web host, sees the requests your browser
makes to it.

### Earlier early-access requests

If you asked for early access through an earlier form and want your request deleted, email
hello@marisstella.app from the address you used.

### Who we are

Maris Stella Labs LLC.
